prompt: Why does modern C++ code run faster than C++03 code on many workloads, even with no algorithm changes?
options: Move semantics avoid expensive copies of large objects
correctAnswer: Move semantics avoid expensive copies of large objects
explanation: C++11 move semantics let the STL transfer rather than copy when it can. Returning a 1MB vector now moves (O(1) pointer swap) instead of copying every byte. Across an entire codebase, this is a major real-world speedup.

prompt: In C++, virtual function calls go through a vtable, costing one indirection compared to direct calls.
explanation: Each polymorphic class has a vtable; each instance has a vptr. Virtual calls index into the vtable. The cost is small (one indirection) but real, and modern CPUs branch-predict it well.

prompt: What technique allows the compiler to elide a copy of a returned object, even before move semantics existed?
explanation: Copy elision (RVO/NRVO) lets the compiler construct the return value directly in the caller's space. C++17 made some forms mandatory.

prompt: Why is the diamond inheritance problem more dangerous in C++ than in Java?
options: C++ has multiple inheritance, where a class can inherit from two classes both deriving from a common base, requiring virtual inheritance to avoid duplicating the base
correctAnswer: C++ has multiple inheritance, where a class can inherit from two classes both deriving from a common base, requiring virtual inheritance to avoid duplicating the base
explanation: Without virtual inheritance, the most-derived class would have two copies of the common base. Modern C++ generally avoids deep multiple inheritance.

prompt: Find the error in this code:
steps: // in C++14 and earlier, 'new Foo' may be evaluated first, then risky() throws
// the raw Foo is never owned by any shared_ptr, so it leaks
explanation: Step 3 is the error. Handing a bare 'new Foo' to the shared_ptr constructor inside a larger call expression leaves an unowned allocation in flight: under C++14 and earlier rules the compiler may evaluate 'new Foo', then evaluate risky(), which throws before the shared_ptr is constructed, and the Foo leaks. C++17 tightened argument evaluation so each argument is fully evaluated before the next, but the fix that works on every standard is std::make_shared<Foo>(), which never exposes a raw owning pointer.

prompt: std::make_shared usually allocates the control block and the managed object together in one allocation, while shared_ptr(new T) does two.
explanation: make_shared is faster (single allocation), better cache locality, and exception-safe. The downside: the managed object's memory isn't released until ALL shared_ptrs AND weak_ptrs are gone (because the control block is in the same allocation).

prompt: What's the main argument for using std::span instead of (pointer, size) parameters in modern C++?
options: span is type-safe and documents intent (a non-owning view of a contiguous range)
correctAnswer: span is type-safe and documents intent (a non-owning view of a contiguous range)
explanation: std::span<T> (C++20) makes 'I want to read/write a contiguous range without owning it' explicit. Replaces (T*, size_t) parameter pairs with a single, less error-prone type.

prompt: What C++ idiom hides implementation details in a forward-declared struct accessed only through a pointer, reducing compile dependencies?
explanation: PIMPL (pointer to implementation) keeps the public header free of private members. Changing the impl doesn't trigger recompilation of consumers — a major build-time win at scale.
